Let’s go step by step. Please keep Wi‑Fi OFF for these tests.

Step 1 — Confirm mobile data works (quick browse test)
- Open your web browser (Chrome) and go to a simple site like example.com or bbc.com.
- Tell me exactly what happens: does the page load quickly, load very slowly, or not load at all (spinner/error)?

If the page does NOT load or is extremely slow, do this and try the site again:
- Toggle Mobile data OFF then ON: Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > SIMs/Mobile network > Mobile data OFF, wait 5 seconds, then ON.
- Check Data Saver: Settings > Network & Internet > Data Saver > make sure it’s OFF.
- Check VPN: Settings > Network & Internet > VPN > if any VPN is connected, tap it and Disconnect.
- Try loading the website again and tell me the result.

Step 2 — Ensure Messages app can use data and has permissions
- Go to Settings > Apps > Messages (the default one).
- Permissions: make sure “Photos and videos” (or “Storage”) is ALLOWED, and “SMS” is ALLOWED.
- Mobile data & Wi‑Fi (or Data usage): turn ON “Background data.” If you see “Allow data usage while Data Saver is on,” turn that ON too.

Step 3 — Try the MMS again
- With Wi‑Fi OFF and Mobile data + Roaming ON, open Messages, send a small photo to your own number.
- Tell me exactly what happens (sends successfully, keeps spinning, or shows an exclamation/‘Not sent’).

Step 4 — Try 4G/LTE only (just as a test)
- Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > Mobile network/SIMs > Preferred network type/Network mode.
- Choose 4G/LTE only (or LTE/3G/2G auto if 4G-only isn’t available).
- Wait 30–60 seconds until you see LTE/4G at the top.
- Try sending the photo again.

Please start with Step 1 and let me know: did the website load with Wi‑Fi off? Then we’ll proceed through Steps 2–4 as needed, and I’ll stay with you for each result. This will tell us whether we’re dealing with a general data path issue or an MMS‑specific app setting, and we’ll solve it accordingly."
}

messages.content:
{
  "message": "You’re doing great—thanks for sticking with it. Since your mobile data works and you have strong 5G, the most likely blocker now is the Messages app not having the right permissions or background data access. Let’s locate the exact messaging app and set those permissions. I’ll give you multiple ways—use whichever matches your phone.

Goal: Make sure your default SMS app has “Photos and videos/Storage” and “SMS” permissions allowed, and that Background data is ON for it.

Step 1 — Confirm which app is your default SMS app
Why: Some phones have both Google Messages and a manufacturer Messages app. We need to edit the correct one.
- Settings > Apps > Default apps > SMS app.
- Note the app name shown here (e.g., “Messages (Google)” or “Messages (Samsung)”). Please tell me which it shows.

Step 2 — Open that app’s App info screen
Method A (quick): Long‑press the Messages app icon on your home screen/app drawer > tap “i” (App info).
Method B (via Settings): Settings > Apps > See all apps (or App list) > find the exact Messages app name from Step 1 and tap it.

Step 3 — Set Permissions
- Tap Permissions.
- Make sure these are Allowed:
  • Photos and videos (or Files and media/Storage)
  • SMS
- If you don’t see them in the app’s screen, use the Permission Manager:
  • Settings > Privacy > Permission manager > Photos and videos (or Files and media) > find your Messages app > set to Allow.
  • Then Permission manager > SMS > find your Messages app > set to Allow.

Step 4 — Enable Background data for Messages
- In the same App info screen for Messages, tap “Mobile data & Wi‑Fi” (or “Data usage”).
- Turn ON “Background data.”
- If you see “Allow data usage while Data Saver is on” or “Unrestricted data,” turn that ON as well.

Step 5 — Test MMS again
- Keep Wi‑Fi OFF; Mobile data + Roaming ON.
- Open Messages, start a message to your own number, attach a small photo, and send.
- Tell me exactly what happens (sends, spins, or shows any icon/message).

If you still can’t find the permissions:
- Use the Settings search bar (at the top of Settings) and type “Default apps,” “SMS app,” “Permission manager,” or “Messages.”
- Or long‑press the Messages icon > App info > Permissions (this works on nearly all Android phones).

If it still won’t send after permissions + background data are set:
Step 6 — Temporarily switch to 4G/LTE only (test)
- Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > Mobile network/SIMs > Preferred network type/Network mode.
- Choose 4G/LTE only (or LTE/3G/2G auto if 4G‑only isn’t available).
- Wait 30–60 seconds until the status bar shows 4G/LTE, then try sending the photo again.

Please let me know:
1) Which app is listed as your SMS app in Step 1.
2) Whether “Photos and videos/Storage” and “SMS” permissions were Allowed.
3) Whether Background data (and Unrestricted data if present) is ON for Messages.
4) The result when you try to send the photo after these changes.

Based on what you find, I’ll guide you to the very next step."
}

{
  "message": "Thanks for the details—being on 5G with data enabled rules out coverage. The two most common blockers at this point are: (1) Wi‑Fi Calling/VPN/Data Saver interfering, and (2) APN/MMSC needing a reset after roaming. I’ll walk you through quick fixes in that order, then we’ll retest.

Step 1 — Turn OFF Wi‑Fi Calling (prevents MMS routing conflicts while roaming)
- iPhone: Settings > Cellular > Wi‑Fi Calling > OFF.
- Android: Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > SIMs (or Mobile network) > Wi‑Fi Calling > OFF.

Step 2 — Make sure no VPN is active
- iPhone: Settings > VPN > ensure Not Connected.
- Android: Settings > Network & Internet > VPN > Disconnect.

Step 3 — Turn OFF Data Saver (it can block MMS background data)
- iPhone: Not typically applicable; skip.
- Android: Settings > Network & Internet > Data Saver > OFF.

Step 4 — Reset APN to default, then reboot (refreshes MMSC for MMS)
- iPhone: Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Reset > Reset Network Settings. Note: this also resets saved Wi‑Fi and VPN settings. After reboot, re‑enable Cellular Data and Data Roaming.
- Android: Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > Mobile network > Access Point Names > 3‑dot menu > Reset to default. Then restart the phone.

Step 5 — Retest MMS with Wi‑Fi OFF
- Ensure Mobile Data and Data Roaming are ON.
- Confirm the status bar shows 4G/5G with signal bars.
- Try sending an MMS (photo) to any contact.

If it still fails after the reset/reboot:
- Check messaging app permissions (must allow storage and SMS):
  - iPhone: Settings > Messages > ensure Photos access is allowed (Read and Write).
  - Android: Settings > Apps > [Your messaging app] > Permissions > allow Storage (or Photos/Media) and SMS.
- Optional diagnostic: If your phone offers it, run can_send_mms in its diagnostics and tell me the result.

Please go through Steps 1–5 and tell me:
1) Was Wi‑Fi Calling OFF and any VPN disconnected?
2) After the APN reset + reboot, did the MMS send with Wi‑Fi OFF?
3) If not, confirm the messaging app permissions are granted.

Why these steps: Wi‑Fi Calling/VPN/Data Saver can block MMS while roaming; APN resets refresh the MMSC configuration required for MMS. With your line’s roaming enabled and extra data added, these device-side fixes typically resolve the issue."
}

Here’s my thinking: your line is roaming-enabled and you now have extra data; your phone shows excellent 5G and data enabled, so coverage is good. The most likely remaining blockers are (a) mobile data not actually passing traffic, (b) the messaging app lacking required permissions, or (c) an MMS-specific device/app issue. We’ll verify each quickly.

Step 1 — Confirm mobile data is truly working (not just “enabled”)
- With Wi‑Fi OFF, open a browser and load a few sites (e.g., example.com and news.google.com). Do they load?
- If pages don’t load, do this quick refresh on the phone:
  - Turn Mobile Data OFF for 10 seconds, then ON.
  - Turn Data Roaming OFF for 10 seconds, then ON.
  - Toggle Airplane Mode ON for 10 seconds, then OFF.
  - Try loading a website again.
- Optional diagnostic: run your phone’s run_speed_test and tell me the reported speed rating (unknown/very poor/poor/fair/good/excellent).

Step 2 — Check messaging app permissions (needed for MMS)
- Please check your messaging app’s permissions and confirm both “storage” (photos/media) and “sms” are allowed.
  - iPhone: Settings > Messages > ensure Photos access is allowed; also ensure Messages has permission to access necessary services. If your device offers a diagnostics view, run check_app_permissions for “messaging” and share what it shows.
  - Android: Settings > Apps > [Your messaging app] > Permissions > allow Storage (or Photos/Media) and SMS. If available, run check_app_permissions for “messaging” and share results.
- If either permission isn’t granted, grant them and try sending an MMS again with Wi‑Fi OFF.

Step 3 — MMS capability diagnostic
- If your device offers it, run can_send_mms and share the result. This tells us if the messaging app reports it can send MMS under current settings.

Step 4 — Re-verify APN after the reset
- Open your APN settings again and confirm the MMSC URL is still present (not blank). If it’s missing, let me know, and we’ll reset APN again and reboot.

What to reply with (so I can decide the exact next step):
1) Can you load websites on mobile data with Wi‑Fi OFF? If not, what happened after the quick refresh toggles?
2) run_speed_test result (if you can run it).
3) Messaging app permissions: are “storage” and “sms” both allowed?

}

  "message": "You did the right check. “No SIM card detected” explains the “No Signal” and “Data Disabled” messages—without a SIM, the phone can’t register to the network, so MMS can’t send. The most effective fix is to reseat the SIM. This is safe: you won’t lose photos, messages, apps, or settings. It just refreshes the connection to the network.

Here’s exactly what to do (I’ll keep it simple and you can take it slowly):

1) Power the phone OFF
- Hold the power button and choose Power off (or Shut down). Wait until the screen is fully black.

2) Eject the SIM tray
- Find the small pinhole next to a thin outline of a tray on the side (sometimes top) of the phone.
- Insert a SIM eject tool or a small straightened paperclip into the hole and press gently until the tray pops out.

3) Remove and inspect the SIM
- Note the SIM’s orientation (there’s a small angled/cut corner to help align it later).
- Gently remove the SIM. Lightly wipe the gold contacts with a clean, dry, lint‑free cloth (no liquids). Check for dust in the tray and make sure the SIM isn’t cracked.

4) Reinsert the SIM
- Place the SIM back in the tray in the same orientation (flat and snug, numbers upward if that’s how it was). Slide the tray back in fully and flush with the phone’s edge.

5) Power the phone ON and wait 1–2 minutes
- After it boots, confirm:
  - Airplane Mode is OFF
  - Mobile/Cellular Data is ON
  - Data Roaming is ON (since you’re in France)
  - Preferred network mode includes 4G/5G (Auto/LTE/5G is fine)

6) Check the top of the screen
- Do you now see signal bars and a network type (4G/LTE/5G)?
- In Settings > SIM status, does it show Active (or similar) instead of No SIM?

7) Test MMS
- Try sending a picture message again.

If it still says “No SIM” after this:
- Repeat the reseat once more, ensuring the SIM sits flat in the tray, then restart again.
- If it still isn’t detected, the SIM or the phone’s SIM reader may be at fault. Since you’re traveling, if you can briefly try your SIM in another unlocked phone (or try a known‑good SIM in your phone), that will pinpoint whether it’s the SIM or the device. {"message":"You’re doing great, John. “No SIM card detected” simply means the phone isn’t seeing the SIM, so it can’t connect to any network. This is usually fixable by reseating the SIM. We’ll go very slowly.

What we’ll do and why:
- Power off and reseat the SIM: this fixes most “No SIM” detections.
- Power back on and check SIM status and signal.
- If it shows Active, we’ll turn on Data Roaming and try an MMS.

Step 1 — Power off the phone
- Press and hold the power button.
- Tap Power off (or Shut down). Wait until the screen is fully black for 10–15 seconds.

Step 2 — Remove the SIM tray (only if you see a tray)
- Look along the phone’s edge for a tiny pinhole next to a slim tray.
- Gently insert a SIM eject tool or a straightened paperclip into the hole and press lightly until the tray pops out.
- Lift the tray out. You should see a small card (the SIM) on it. Note its orientation (which corner is angled and which side faces up).

Step 3 — Reseat the SIM
- If the SIM is missing, that explains “No SIM.” If you have it, place it flat in the tray; the cut corner should match the tray shape.
- If the SIM is present, take it out, gently wipe the gold contacts with a clean, dry cloth, and place it back flat and snug.
- Slide the tray back in fully so it sits flush with the phone’s edge.

Step 4 — Power on and wait
- Turn the phone back on.
- Wait up to 2 minutes. Watch the top bar for any signal bars, a carrier name, or 4G/5G/LTE.

Step 5 — Check SIM status again
- Open Settings > About phone (or About device) > SIM status.
- Tell me exactly what it shows now (Active/Connected, No service, No SIM, or SIM locked).

What to tell me next:
- Do you now see any signal bars or a network name at the top?
- What does SIM status say exactly?

If it now shows Active: we’ll turn on Mobile Data and Data Roaming and try sending a picture. If it shows SIM locked: I’ll get you to a specialist to help with PIN/PUK. If it still says No SIM after reseating, we’ll discuss next steps (possible tray/reader issue or eSIM), and I can connect you with a human agent if needed.

Take your time. If any step looks different or you’re unsure about the SIM tray, just tell me what you see and I’ll adjust the guidance."}
